title: TA8-02154
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: XXXXX XXXXX, a citizen of Colombia, claims to be in need of refugee protection pursuant to sections 96 and 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).1 ALLEGATIONS

The claimant is a 31-year-old man originally from XXXXX, Antioquia, where he worked for the XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX products company supporting the Ecuador market. He said that, in XXXXX 2007, a man from the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC) came to his office and demanded that he let the FARC use certain of the company's XXXXX. Fearful, he said that he applied for a Canadian visa, good for XXXXX, 2007. Five weeks after the incident, the FARC man showed up at his home and explained to him that the XXXXX would be needed soon for a XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX to Ecuador, and the FARC wanted him to arrange a meeting with the XXXXX in two months. He spoke to his boss about going to study French in Montreal and left Colombia on XXXXX, 2008.

The panel finds that the claimant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection for the reason that the panel does not find the material aspects of the claimant's story to be credible or his fear to be well founded. Alternatively, the panel finds there is a viable internal flight alternative (IFA) for him in Colombia. ANALYSIS Identity
The claimant's identity has been established by certified copies of his Colombian passport and other identification documents as tendered into evidence.2 Nexus

Based on the panel's analysis on credibility/well-foundedness of his fear (below), the panel finds this claim to have no connection to a Convention ground and proceeded with the analyses under section 97. However, even if there is such a connection, the following analyses apply to section 96, as well. Credibility / Well-foundedness of the Claimant's Fear

The determinative issue in this case is credibility as to the well-foundedness of the claimant's fear. The panel finds the claimant's story not to be wholly credible in its material aspects due to the following reasons.

He said that he did not report the FARC contacts and threats to the police, as the FARC man warned him not to. However, the panel finds this strange because he says that the FARC has infiltrated the police and would know about any report he made. If this were the case, it does not make sense that the FARC would be so concerned about him making a report to the police if their infiltrators could simply quash or stymie any investigation on his complaint. The panel takes a negative inference from this and views this, on a balance of probabilities, as an embellishment to his claim.

Furthermore, the claimant did not receive any sufragio (death note) or file any complaint to authorities and, therefore, has absolutely nothing to corroborate his claim that he was targeted by the FARC. Although, oral testimony is viewed with a lot of weight, the lack or complete absence of any direct or indirect corroborating evidence does not help when assessing the veracity of the claimant's story, particularly when the onus to prove his claim rests on him. The panel draws a negative inference from this total lack of corroborating evidence and, consequently, believes that, on a balance of probabilities, his story that he is a target of the FARC is not true.

Furthermore, the FARC, in this case, does not appear to have approached his boss or colleagues as a back up for their demand to use the company XXXXX, just in case the claimant refused to go through with the plan. The panel finds this perplexing and, again, draws a negative inference on this lack of foresight or planning on the part of the FARC. Furthermore, the claimant's parents and younger brother still live in the same place in XXXXX and have not been approached by the FARC looking for him. It is known that the FARC usually goes against family members of their targets, who have crossed or eluded them.3 In this case, no such confrontation or harassment on his family members even occurred. Based on this and taking into account the foregoing discussion, the panel does not believe that, on a balance of probabilities, the claimant is a target of the FARC. Internal Flight Alternative (IFA)

If the foregoing were not the issue, IFA would be in Bogota, the country's capital, a megalopolis of more than 8 million people, about four times the size of Toronto. The panel finds that the claimant, who had been living in XXXXX during his alleged problems with the FARC, can relocate to Bogota and live among its large mass of people and out of sight of the FARC, without necessarily having to hide.

In support of that, the panel cites the following points with respect to the current National Documentation Package on Colombia,4 as follows: * While the previous 2005 UNHCR report of March 2005, in paragraph 58, said that, "The irregular armed groups have the capacity to track down victims throughout Colombia and indeed have done so frequently in the past," such reference no longer exists in the current report published four years later by the same agency. The panel is satisfied that this reference has been removed since it no longer applies. * Of particular interest in the current Exhibit R/A-1 are two reports by the International Crisis Group 4.1 from April 2008 and 4.5 from March 2009. Both are recent and all statements fully documented. Furthermore, the Group is guided by well-known and respected international personalities, including a former Prime Minister of Canada and an internationally recognized Canadian jurist. * The first report outlines the problems that the current Uribe government has created for the FARC since 2002, as follows: o Many experienced commanders have been killed by security forces, assassinated by other insurgents, or died. This has severely disrupted communications and cohesion within the FARC organization. o No Colombian political party supports the FARC any longer as a legitimate left-wing force. o After six years of sustained military offensives, the FARC's command structure is believed to be faltering due to a lack of internal communication. o The country's security forces believe that the FARC is less operational, i.e. in 2007, there were only between 9,000 and 11,000 fighters supporting the FARC as opposed to approximately 19,000 in 2002, and only 10 of its former 71 fronts are currently active. o The FARC is attempting to regain legitimacy in the rural population by avoiding harm to civilians while focusing on high impact military targets. * The more recent 2009 report notes, as follows: o Key units of the FARC have withdrawn to the jungle and mountains. o Even though the FARC has replaced its leaders in its senior command, coordination between senior and mid-ranking commanders is difficult. o Demobilized former fighters have moved into big cities to decrease the risk of being targeted by the FARC. o Government security forces have pushed the FARC out of heavily populated areas and are regaining control of road arteries. o Areas where the FARC is strong and active are noted - western Meta, Putumayo, high mountain ranges or tropical jungle. (None of these include large urban populations). o Government security forces are preventing the FARC from attempting to regain status in urban areas through terrorism. Police have seized caches of explosives in the outskirts and FARC commandos have been arrested when attempting to penetrate cities. The first two complete paragraphs of page 12 indicate that FARC urban structures have been disrupted; however, insurgents remain active in Cali and Buenaventura. Now that the FARC works in independent cells, support networks have been progressively weakened. In the early 2000's, urban fronts were driven out of cities like Bogota, Medellin, Cali and Cucuta. Security forces have made FARC logistics vulnerable to interception and exert tight control via checkpoints on roads and rivers that lead from combat areas. o Extortion may have increased but is under-reported. Individuals may be using the FARC's name as a means to extract extortion, and this brings up the question that common criminals are likely committing these crimes and, therefore, the situation has moved away from nexus to criminality. o Section 8 (page 15) states that, in urban areas, FARC support has vanished. Tens of thousands marched in Bogota against the FARC in March 2008. o Government security forces have increased to more than 400,000 in 2007 and have been successful in forcing the FARC to retreat. Since 2007, security forces have expanded their presence in rural areas. * The only 2008 reference to an incident in a large urban centre occurred in September when a car bomb killed four civilians in front of a court house in Cali. This type of incident would not generally be considered a targeted killing.

In summary, the panel is satisfied that the FARC has moved away its bases of operations from urban areas to rural areas with headquarters in the mountains or jungles and no longer has the ability to track an individual from one area to another, due to surveillance by government security forces and their ability to interrupt communications.

Based on the foregoing, the panel finds that there is adequate, if not necessarily effective, state protection in Bogota. The panel further finds that Bogota would be a reasonable IFA for the claimant considering that it has a large population of over 8 million and opportunities for social services that a well-developed capital city of the country can offer its inhabitants. The panel finds that Bogota would meet both requirements for a viable IFA for the claimant.

Consequently, based on the totality of the evidence adduced, including counsel's submissions, the panel is not persuaded to believe that the claimant faces persecution on a Convention ground or a risk to life, or of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, or a danger of torture, should he be returned to Colombia today.

The Refugee Protection Division, therefore, determines that XXXXX XXXXX is neither a Convention refugee within the meaning of section 96 of the IRPA nor a person in need of protection under subsection 97(1). His claim is, therefore, rejected. (SIGNED) "W. LIM" W.
